title: Cap. X Arg. VII: against Christ-death as a cast lot — Isa. liii. 10 promises Christ a church if he lays down his soul as a sacrifice
latin: At quicquid isti tenent, est prorsus alienum a Theologia, et Scripturis contrarium, mortem Christi fuisse quasi aleam jactam, ita ut posita anima sua, an quisquam per mortem ejus salvus fieret, ex contingentia liberi hominum arbitrii prorsus penderet. Longe aliter Isaias, Isa. liii. 10. Si posuerit animam suam hostiam pro peccato, semen longaevum videbit. Deus igitur promittit Christo Ecclesiam, si animam posuerit hostiam pro peccato.
pass_a: But whatsoever these hold is utterly alien from Theology, and contrary to the Scriptures: that the death of Christ was as it were a lot cast, so that, his soul having been laid down, whether anyone should be made safe through his death would hang wholly upon the contingency of men’s free will. Far otherwise Isaiah, Isa. liii. 10. If he shall have laid down his soul a sacrifice for sin, he shall see a long-lived seed. God therefore promises unto Christ a Church, if he shall have laid down his soul a sacrifice for sin.
pass_b: But whatever they hold is wholly alien to theology and contrary to Scripture: that Christ’s death was like a lot cast, so that—his soul once laid down—whether anyone would be saved by that death hung wholly on the contingency of human free will. Isaiah speaks far otherwise (Isa. liii. 10): If he shall lay down his soul as a sacrifice for sin, he shall see a long-lived seed. So God promises Christ a church if he lays down his soul as a sacrifice for sin.

title: Cap. X Arg. VII: fulfillment of the promise not from uncertain free will but from the firmest decree and matching operation
latin: Quod autem Deus promisit Filio, ejus impletio non ex incerta operatione humani arbitrii, sed ex firmissimo divinae voluntatis decreto, et operatione eidem decreto respondente arcessenda est.
pass_a: But what God promised unto the Son, the fulfilling of it is not to be fetched from the uncertain operation of human free will, but from the firmest decree of the divine will, and from an operation answering unto the same decree.
pass_b: What God promised the Son must be fetched not from the uncertain working of human free will, but from the firmest decree of the divine will and from an operation that answers to that decree.

lemmas.gloss: promise fulfilled by decree not free will

title: Cap. X Arg. VII: Augustine De praedest. sanct. 10 — he promised from his predestination, not from our will’s power; he makes us do what he commands
latin: Horsum facit illud Augustini, De praedest. sanctorum, cap. 10. Non de nostrae voluntatis potestate, sed de sua praedestinatione promisit. Promisit enim quod ipse facturus fuerat, non quod homines: quia etsi faciunt homines bona quae pertinent ad colendum Deum, ipse facit ut illi faciant quae praecepit, non illi faciunt ut ipse faciat quod promisit: alioquin ut Dei promissa compleantur, non in Dei sed in hominum esset potestate.
pass_a: Unto this belongs that of Augustine, De praedest. sanctorum, cap. 10. He promised not of the power of our will, but of his own predestination. For he promised what he himself was going to do, not what men: because although men do good things which pertain unto worshipping God, he himself makes that they do what he has commanded; they do not make that he do what he has promised: otherwise, that God’s promises should be fulfilled would be not in God’s power but in men’s.
pass_b: Here belongs Augustine (De praedestinatione sanctorum 10): He promised not from the power of our will, but from his own predestination. For he promised what he himself would do, not what men would do: though men do the goods that belong to worshipping God, he makes them do what he commanded; they do not make him do what he promised—otherwise the fulfillment of God’s promises would lie not in God’s power but in men’s.

lemmas.gloss: promise from predestination not our will
God makes men do what he commanded

title: Cap. X Arg. VII close: foresight-election leaves God’s promise, and whether Christ is Head with members, to free will — firmness is in predestination, not bare foresight
latin: Videtis vim argumenti; Electio et reprobatio ex praevisione actuum humanorum contingenter prodeuntium aut non-prodeuntium e voluntate humana, libero hominum arbitrio committit utrum Dei promissio implebitur necne, utrum Christus morte sua Ecclesiam aliquam sibi acquiret an secus, uno verbo, utrum Christus erit Caput sine membris, Redemptor sine redemptis, Servator sine servatis, necne, quae omnia in divina praedestinatione et operatione habent suam firmitatem et infallibilem certitudinem, non in nuda praevisione, quid homines pro libertate arbitrii sui acturi sint, aut non acturi.
pass_a: Ye see the force of the argument; Election and reprobation from foresight of human acts contingently proceeding or not-proceeding from the human will commits unto men’s free will whether God’s promise shall be fulfilled or not, whether Christ by his death shall acquire unto himself some Church or otherwise, in a word, whether Christ shall be a Head without members, a Redeemer without redeemed, a Saviour without saved, or not—all which things have their firmness and infallible certainty in divine predestination and operation, not in bare foresight of what men by the liberty of their will are going to do, or not going to do.
pass_b: See the force of the argument: election and reprobation from foresight of human acts that contingently proceed or fail to proceed from the human will hands over to free will whether God’s promise will be fulfilled, whether Christ by his death will gain a church for himself or not—in a word, whether Christ will be a Head without members, a Redeemer without redeemed, a Savior without saved. All that has its firmness and infallible certainty in divine predestination and operation, not in bare foresight of what men will or will not do by free will.

lemmas.lemma: Caput sine membris ... Servator sine servatis
lemmas.gloss: foresight scheme risks Head without members
certainty in predestination not bare foresight

title: Cap. X Arg. VII→VIII open: if reprobation only from antecedent unbelief, all infants dying before free will—even pagans—must be elect and saved
latin: Posita reprobatione non nisi ex antecedente infidelitate et contemtu actuali sive neglectu gratiae Divinae, necesse est ut ponamus tanquam certum fide catholica, omnes infantes, etiam Paganorum, qui moriuntur ante usum liberi arbitrii, electos esse et salvos fore. Ratio in promptu est, Quia tales infidelitatis reatum ex contemptu Evangelii et gratiae Divinae contrahere nondum potuerunt.
pass_a: Reprobation having been laid down as only from antecedent unbelief and actual contempt or neglect of Divine grace, it is necessary that we lay down as certain by catholic faith that all infants, even of Pagans, who die before the use of free will, are elect and will be safe. The reason is at hand, Because such could not yet contract the guilt of unbelief from contempt of the Gospel and of Divine grace.
pass_b: Grant reprobation only from antecedent unbelief plus actual contempt or neglect of divine grace, and catholic faith would have to treat as certain that every infant who dies before free will—even a pagan’s—is elect and will be saved. Why? Such a child could not yet incur unbelief’s guilt from scorning the Gospel and divine grace.

lemmas.lemma: omnes infantes ... electos esse et salvos
lemmas.gloss: foresight-reprobation forces all dying infants elect

title: Cap. X Arg. VIII: the Church never dared that — infants outside the Church born unclean and debtors of eternal death unless secret mercy intervene
latin: At Ecclesia Christi nunquam hoc ausa est statuere: sed e contra, de statu infantium extra Ecclesiam natorum in se considerato pronunciat, Omnes nasci impuros, omnes mori aeternae mortis reos, nisi arcana nobis minime revelata Dei misericordia quibusdam extra ordinem succurrat.
pass_a: But the Church of Christ never dared to establish this: but on the contrary, concerning the state of infants born outside the Church considered in itself, she pronounces that All are born unclean, all die guilty of eternal death, unless the secret mercy of God, by no means revealed unto us, succour certain ones out of order.
pass_b: But Christ’s church never dared to settle that. On the contrary, of infants born outside the church considered in themselves she pronounces: All are born unclean; all die debtors of eternal death, unless God’s secret mercy—not revealed to us—helps certain ones beyond the ordinary order.

lemmas.gloss: church never taught all dying infants elect
born unclean; debtors of eternal death

title: Cap. X Arg. VIII: Augustine stops Pelagians/Semipelagians with elect/reprobate infants; De praed. sanct. 12 and De bono pers. 11 — God helps those little ones he chose before the world
latin: Hoc argumento ab infantium quorundam electione, quorundam reprobatione, petito Augustinus passim obstruit ora Pelagianorum et Semipelagianorum, qui hoc discrimen electorum et non-electorum ad praevisos actus humanarum voluntatum sive bonos sive malos revocarunt, sicuti et Arminiani jam revocant. Infinitum esset omnia Augustini testimonia in hanc sententiam accumulare. Videte De Praed. Sanct. cap. 12, De bono persev. cap. 11. ubi diserte asserit, Deus parvulis, quibus vult, etiam non volentibus neque currentibus subvenire; quos scilicet ante constitutionem mundi elegit; quibus vero non vult non subvenire, de quibus in sua praedestinatione occulte quidem, sed juste aliud judicavit.
pass_a: By this argument drawn from the election of certain infants, the reprobation of certain, Augustine everywhere stops the mouths of the Pelagians and Semipelagians, who recalled this discrimination of elect and non-elect unto the foreseen acts of human wills, whether good or evil, just as the Arminians now also recall it. It would be endless to heap up all Augustine’s testimonies unto this sentence. See De Praed. Sanct. cap. 12, De bono persev. cap. 11. where he expressly asserts, God succours little ones, whom he wills, even when not willing nor running; whom namely he elected before the foundation of the world; but those whom he wills not, he does not succour, concerning whom in his predestination he judged otherwise, secretly indeed, but justly.
pass_b: From this argument—election of some infants, reprobation of others—Augustine everywhere stops the mouths of Pelagians and Semipelagians, who traced the divide of elect and non-elect to foreseen acts of human wills, good or evil, as the Arminians now do. It would be endless to pile up all his witnesses on this point. See De praedestinatione sanctorum 12 and De bono perseverantiae 11, where he expressly asserts: God helps the little ones he wills, even when they are not willing or running—those he chose before the foundation of the world; those he does not will, he does not help, of whom in his predestination he judged otherwise, secretly but justly.

lemmas.lemma: parvulis quibus vult ... ante constitutionem mundi
lemmas.gloss: helps chosen little ones before the world

title: Cap. X Arg. VIII close: Prosper — in infants neither prior merit nor future devotion is chosen; catholic sense: many die debtors of eternal death; Arminius rejected
latin: Prosper etiam eandem sententiam ubique amplectitur: De lib. arbitr. ad Ruffin. In infantibus nec praecedens eligitur, nec futura devotio. In Epistola ad Augustinum, Parvuli, inquit, nullas adhuc habentes voluntates, nullas proprias actiones, non sine Dei judicio secernuntur, cum alii per regenerationem inter caelestis regni assumantur heredes, alii sine Baptismo inter mortis perpetuae transeant debitores. Denique ut brevi absolvam, constans fuit totius Ecclesiae catholicae sententia, (reservatis semper Deo arcanis suis) Infantes omnes nasci reos mortis aeternae, multos non regeneratos, et transire debitores mortis aeternae, ut ex Prospero accepimus. Arminii igitur sententia, quae reprobationem nullam concedit nisi ex praevisa reprobatorum infidelitate et perseverantia in eadem, fuit semper totius Ecclesiae orthodoxae calculo rejecta et condemnata.
pass_a: Prosper also everywhere embraces the same sentence: De lib. arbitr. ad Ruffin. In infants neither what precedes is chosen, nor future devotion. In the Epistle unto Augustine, Little ones, he says, as yet having no wills, no proper actions, are not without God’s judgment severed, when some through regeneration are taken up among the heirs of the heavenly kingdom, others without Baptism pass among the debtors of perpetual death. Finally that I may briefly finish, it was the constant sentence of the whole catholic Church (God’s secrets being always reserved unto him) that All infants are born guilty of eternal death, many not regenerated, and pass as debtors of eternal death, as we have received from Prosper. Arminius’s sentence therefore, which grants no reprobation except from the foreseen unbelief of the reprobate and perseverance in the same, was always rejected and condemned by the reckoning of the whole orthodox Church.
pass_b: Prosper everywhere holds the same (De libero arbitrio ad Ruffinum): In infants neither what precedes is chosen, nor future devotion. In his letter to Augustine: Little ones, he says, still having no wills and no acts of their own, are not parted without God’s judgment—some through regeneration taken up among heirs of the heavenly kingdom, others without baptism passing among debtors of perpetual death. In short, the whole catholic church’s constant sense (always reserving God’s secrets to him) has been: All infants are born debtors of eternal death; many pass unregenerate as debtors of eternal death—as we have it from Prosper. So Arminius’s view, which grants no reprobation except from the reprobate’s foreseen unbelief and perseverance in it, was always rejected and condemned by the whole orthodox church’s reckoning.

lemmas.lemma: In infantibus nec praecedens ... nec futura
lemmas.gloss: Prosper: no prior merit or future devotion chosen
